title: Path sensitivity & KV serialization: deterministic p99 workshop - Polaris Dataworks
topics: KV cache serialization and shard affinity
summary: Deep dive into root causes of recurrent p99 spikes. We walked through KV serialization across shard boundaries, network hop amplification for VPC egress, streaming vs non-streaming latency profiles, and mitigations: hotkey sharding, per-route streaming configs, cache pinning, and quantization-aware kernel choices. Agreed to run 48-hour benchmark and share config diffs.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-25 15:00 UTC / Duration ~62 minutes / Recording: on
Attendees: Jamie Ortega, Priya Malhotra, Andre Lewis (Redwood); Ethan Zhou, Riya Kapoor, Markus Voss, Sofia Marin (Polaris)

00:00:03 Jamie Ortega: okay thanks everyone for joining, um we're gonna jump in. quick agenda — reproduce the p99 spikes, walk the path, propose mitigations.
00:00:15 Markus Voss: great, yeah we've been seeing these intermittent fus spikes, p99s jump from 180ms to 1.2s on text-gen paths. it's killing real-time features.
00:00:27 Priya Malhotra: can you clarify — is that across streaming endpoints or non-streaming?
00:00:33 Ethan Zhou: both, but more frequent on streaming. non-streaming sometimes bursts during cold-cache windows.
00:00:40 Andre Lewis: interesting, streaming usually helps tail because you emit early, but if there's a multi-hop network serialization it can amplify.
00:00:50 Riya Kapoor: our infra is VPC peered to Redwood Private edge in us-east-1, with cross-account NLBs. we also have on-prem clusters for sensitive workloads.
00:01:03 Jamie Ortega: ok let's start with a short readout from you guys — what's the shortest repro you have? what traffic percentage sees the spike?
00:01:12 Ethan Zhou: about 3% of requests in production see the spike. we have request IDs if you want them. pattern: user prompt small (<64 tokens), then model expands 600+ tokens or streaming tokens, and p99 hits.
00:01:28 Priya Malhotra: got it. that fits a KV path-length amplification: the KV cache has to be pulled and possibly reshuffled across shards, plus prefix cache misses.
00:01:37 Sofia Marin: can you explain shard reshuffle? we're on 32 KV shards, affinity by request hash but occasionally a hotkey shifts due to autoscaler restart.
00:01:49 Priya Malhotra: yeah so if a hot prefix is moved during autoscale events, subsequent requests go to a different host, and the runtime serializes the KV state to the serving host. that copy + network hop can add 200-400ms. if it also hits disk (cold state), it becomes >1s.
00:02:10 Ethan Zhou: we do see autoscale churn around business-hours peaks, but not always. sometimes it happens on small maintenance windows.
00:02:17 Andre Lewis: another amplifying factor — streaming vs non-streaming: streaming keeps a thin loop on the client side but every token still needs KV lookups for past context. if the first few tokens are delayed because the KV shard is remote, the stream appears choppy. non-streaming hides it until final return but p99 still spikes.
00:02:38 Markus Voss: should we move to pinning shards? we have concerns about cost and capacity.
00:02:44 Priya Malhotra: pinning hot shards is usually best for stable hotkeys. Redwood has an option to pin shard affinity per route, that avoids serialization but reduces flexibility for autoscaling. a middle ground is warm-standby replicas for specific shards.
00:02:58 Riya Kapoor: what about prefix cache? we use prefix KV for user histories, but it's fairly large. if we increase prefix eviction TTL will that blow memory?
00:03:07 Priya Malhotra: yes, increasing TTL or keeping more KV in RAM reduces misses but increases memory. there's also incremental prefix compression and selective caching: keep the last N turns only.
00:03:18 Jamie Ortega: let's annotate the taxonomy: source types for p99 — (1) network hop serialization (KV/resend), (2) disk-backed cold loads, (3) scheduling/pipeline stalls from batching windows, (4) quantization-induced slow paths on CPU/GPU handoff. any additions?
00:03:34 Ethan Zhou: also large fanout requests where one request fans out to many microservices for enrichment — that multiplies network hops.
00:03:41 Andre Lewis: good point. fanout + synchronous blocking contributes a lot. we usually recommend asynchronous enrichment or pre-enrich before model calls.
00:03:51 00:04:02 Speaker 1: [inaudible] sorry, Markus?
00:04:05 Markus Voss: i was gonna say, the majority of those 3% correlate to a single enrichment service that we call synchronously for entity resolution.
00:04:13 Priya Malhotra: that's a smoking gun. if enrichment calls are in the critical path, any spike there will be reflected in model p99. consider parallelizing or caching resolution results.
00:04:25 Ethan Zhou: okay we'll map that flow.
00:04:30 Priya Malhotra: moving on — batching windows. Redwood's continuous batching tries to fill tokens into micro-batches, but aggressive batching increases head-of-line latency for short requests. Did you set max batch latency?
00:04:44 Riya Kapoor: we left batch defaults.
00:04:47 Andre Lewis: default conservative batch window is tuned for throughput. for low-latency endpoints you need smaller max-latency and smaller max-batch-size, or enable streaming per-token emit which reduces perceived latency but may cost more tokens due to overhead.
00:05:01 Ethan Zhou: does streaming increase cost?
00:05:04 Priya Malhotra: marginally, because of framing/overhead and slightly different runtime paths, but usually the UX benefits outweigh cost for interactive features. Cost tradeoff depends on request lengths and token rates.
00:05:17 Jamie Ortega: let's dive into quantization: you mentioned different kernels for 4-bit vs 8-bit, Markus?
00:05:23 Markus Voss: we've tried static 4-bit quant on internal models to save GPU memory. in some scenarios the kernel falls back to CPU for certain ops, causing a cross-device hop that kills p99.
00:05:34 Priya Malhotra: exactly — quantization changes operator selection. some fused attention kernels don't have optimized int4 paths and cause GPU->CPU transfer for a small subgraph. That transfer plus synchronization can add 100-300ms. Redwood Optimize has a quantization compatibility profile we can run to detect these slow paths.
00:05:52 Ethan Zhou: can we get a quick report on our model?
00:05:56 Priya Malhotra: yes we'll run the compatibility scan in the benchmark harness. Andre will try a 8-bit run as a comparison — often 8-bit avoids fallback.
00:06:07 Jamie Ortega: network hop implications for VPC/on-prem — can you sketch your topology, Riya?
00:06:12 Riya Kapoor: sure, traffic from our app cluster routes to a peering VPC, then through a NAT + NLB to the Redwood Private endpoint sitting in our account, then to the inference nodes. On-prem has an egress over VPN.
00:06:26 Priya Malhotra: each additional NAT/NLB can add 10-40ms and increase jitter. For critical low-p95 targets we advise minimizing synchronous proxies in the critical path and prefer direct peering or AWS PrivateLink.
00:06:39 Sofia Marin: we're using cross-account NLB because of team constraints. is PrivateLink a drop-in?
00:06:45 Andre Lewis: mostly yes; sometimes IAM and Cert diffs exist, but PrivateLink reduces hop count and provides stable egress performance, which helps p99.
00:06:55 Ethan Zhou: we also saw periodic 500s from auth when a cert rotated — that caused retransmits and higher tail.
00:07:01 Priya Malhotra: cert rotations causing transient auth errors are classic; ensure graceful cert reloads and backoff retries in client. Redwood's SDK does exponential backoff by default but the client's retries may not be idempotent.
00:07:15 Jamie Ortega: ok let's pull diagnostics: what traces/logs do you have?
00:07:19 Ethan Zhou: we have open-telemetry traces with spans for enrichment, kv-get, model-infer, and egress. sample traces uploaded.
00:07:25 Priya Malhotra: perfect, that's the level we need. For the 48h run, please keep full traces for the top 1% requests. we'll instrument per-hop latencies and overlay kernel selection logs.
00:07:36 Jamie Ortega: now some quick proposed mitigations — high-impact, low-friction first. Priya?
00:07:40 Priya Malhotra: (1) Pin top hotkeys or use warm standby shards. (2) Move enrichment out of critical path or cache enrichment responses. (3) Reduce max-batch-latency for interactive routes or enable per-token streaming. (4) Run quantization compatibility scan and prefer 8-bit if it avoids cross-device fallbacks. (5) Reduce network hops via PrivateLink or remove NLB in critical path.
00:08:02 Riya Kapoor: for pinning, who owns that config?
00:08:05 Andre Lewis: Redwood can suggest per-route config; we'll share sample YAML and a canary plan.
00:08:10 Ethan Zhou: can we run a canary with 2% of traffic for 24 hours?
00:08:14 Jamie Ortega: yes, we'll propose a canary: pin two shards, small batch-window change, and async enrichment toggle. We'll provide rollback steps.
00:08:24 Markus Voss: what about metrics? which dashboards to watch?
00:08:27 Priya Malhotra: p95/p99 latency per-route, per-host KV miss rate, network egress lat distribution, kernel fallback counts, and CPU/GPU transfer ops. We'll share a dashboard link.
00:08:40 Ethan Zhou: any quick wins for immediate relief?
00:08:43 Priya Malhotra: throttle enrichment or switch to cached enrichment for the critical route — that should cut the current spikes by 60-80% in many cases. Also reduce max-batch-latency for the route.
00:08:55 Riya Kapoor: we'll do cached enrichment and report back.
00:08:58 00:09:05 Speaker 2: [crosstalk] sorry, one more Q on serialization: is the KV copy atomic? does it block other requests?
00:09:12 Priya Malhotra: the runtime streams KV through a delta-serialization; it can block serving for the target shard for a short critical section. Large serializations will increase queuing. We mitigate by zero-copy for warm-hot shards or by sharding the prefix cache more granularly.
00:09:29 Markus Voss: what's the recommended shard count? we had 32, we could do 128.
00:09:33 Andre Lewis: more shards reduce per-shard memory and allow more parallelism, but increase cross-shard fanout for global lookups. There's a tradeoff. For heavy hotkeys, increase shard count and ensure affinity for the hot prefix.
00:09:45 Jamie Ortega: ok wrapping up — quick recap of factual next steps.
00:09:50 Jamie Ortega: Redwood to send benchmark harness and YAML examples. Polaris to run 48h baseline and upload traces. Polaris to implement cached enrichment for a canary. Redwood to run quantization compatibility scan on their test model. We'll reconvene after results.
00:10:05 Ethan Zhou: sounds good.
00:10:08 Markus Voss: thanks everyone.

[remainder of call: 52 minutes of Q/A and tracing walkthroughs — detailed spans examined, assorted log excerpts, and configuration diffs shared. Some sections redacted for security in share.]

55:32 Priya Malhotra: i pasted a sample config in chat: https://redwood.ai/configs/pinning-example.yaml and a benchmark starter: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/p99-harness. also a quantization note: https://redwood.ai/docs/quant-compat
55:50 Ethan Zhou: uploaded traces to shared drive: https://drive.company/polaris/p99-traces/2026-06-25
55:58 Jamie Ortega: agreed. we'll set the follow-up for 2026-07-12 to review 48h results.
56:10 Riya Kapoor: can you also send SOC2 / network diagrams?
56:15 Jamie Ortega: yes — will attach SOC2 summary and PrivateLink guide.
56:22 Andre Lewis: small note — when you do 8-bit runs, tag them so we can isolate fallback counts.
56:29 Markus Voss: thanks everyone, bye.
56:32 call ended
questions: How does shard reshuffle cause serialization?
Streaming vs non-streaming: which reduces tail?
What network hops add the most jitter?
How does quantization lead to cross-device fallbacks?
